title: The Baader-Meinhof phenomenon
hook: You learn a new word, and suddenly it seems to be everywhere you look.
peek: Learn a new word, notice a car model or hear of a band, and soon it seems to show up everywhere. It was there all along. The odd name for this comes from a newspaper letter in 1994.
lede: You learn an unfamiliar word, and within days you meet it three more times. It feels like the world has started using it. In fact it was there all along, and your attention has simply started catching it. Linguists call this the frequency illusion, but many people know it by a stranger name taken from a 1994 newspaper letter.

bullets.opening: The St. Paul Pioneer Press letter
bullets.text: In 1994 a reader wrote to the Minnesota paper after hearing the name of the Baader-Meinhof group, a 1970s West German militant group, twice in one day. Other readers wrote in with their own examples, and the name stuck.
In 2005 the Stanford linguist proposed the plainer name on the blog Language Log. Many writers now prefer it, since the effect has nothing to do with the group itself.

Zwicky described two parts. Selective attention makes you notice what is new to you, so each sighting registers. Confirmation bias then counts the hits and forgets the many days without one, so the pattern feels real.
